passage: Associations between cadence and spatiotemporal gait characteristics were examined across the population studied. The relationship between step rate and measures of running mechanics has been the subject of considerable investigation, with findings demonstrating varied associations depending on the imposed constraints and individual characteristics of the cohort.

Ground contact time was examined in relation to running velocity and gait mechanics. Evidence regarding the magnitude of contact phase duration and its relationship to other kinematic variables has been mixed, with inconsistent findings reported across different study designs.

The flight phase duration was investigated as a correlate of running speed and rhythmic gait properties. Findings regarding aerial time have varied in the literature, suggesting that multiple biomechanical mechanisms may influence this temporal parameter.

The duty factor—the ratio of contact time to stride time—was examined as an indicator of gait classification and loading distribution. Associations between this normalized contact parameter and other biomechanical variables have demonstrated moderate to trivial relationships across populations studied.

Stride length was evaluated in relation to velocity, cadence, and mechanical efficiency metrics. The magnitude of this spatiotemporal variable and its associations with kinematic patterns have been examined, though findings regarding optimal stride amplitude remain inconsistent across methodological approaches.

Vertical oscillation of the centre of mass was examined as a measure of running mechanics and metabolic efficiency. Evidence regarding the relationship between vertical displacement and other biomechanical variables has been mixed, with correlations varying depending on locomotor context and measurement approach.

The vertical ratio—vertical oscillation normalized to step length—was investigated as a dimensionless descriptor of running style. Associations between this normalized parameter and movement quality have been examined, though findings have demonstrated variable relationships across different populations and conditions.

Foot landing position relative to the centre of mass was examined as a potential mechanism influencing lower limb loading and braking forces. Evidence regarding the magnitude of overstriding and its association with injury risk and performance outcomes has been inconsistent across the literature.

Foot strike characteristics, including foot inclination angle and rearfoot-to-forefoot strike patterns, were examined in relation to impact biomechanics. Findings regarding the association between foot contact angle and lower limb loading have varied considerably, suggesting that strike pattern classifications alone may not fully capture the complexity of ground contact mechanics.

Sagittal plane knee kinematics at initial contact were examined as a potential determinant of impact loading and shock attenuation. Associations between knee flexion angle at footstrike and measures of lower limb stress have been investigated, with findings demonstrating moderate but inconsistent correlations across different running populations and velocities.

Forward postural lean and trunk inclination were examined in relation to running mechanics and energy transfer. Evidence regarding associations between trunk flexion angle and other kinematic variables has been mixed, with the magnitude of relationships varying depending on speed, terrain, and measurement methodology.
